title: Connecting minerals to meals: Africa’s missed agricultural link
body:
The narrative around Africa’s agricultural potential is often framed almost entirely in terms of land. We are frequently reminded that the continent holds about 65% of the world’s uncultivated arable land—roughly 874 million hectares, a landmass larger than Europe and the Americas combined (https://lnkd.in/ewjbnNpf).

But land alone does not grow food.

What is far less discussed is that Africa’s agricultural potential also lies beneath the soil, in its vast endowment of agro-minerals—the phosphates, potash, natural gas, and limestone that underpin modern agricultural productivity. These resources are the foundational inputs for fertilizers, soil conditioning, and sustained yield growth in modern agriculture.

This disconnect has produced a striking paradox: Africa imports most of the fertilizers it needs while exporting the raw minerals required to produce them. The result is high input costs for farmers, low and volatile productivity, and persistent vulnerability to global supply shocks.

The future of African agriculture, therefore, is not only about how much land it has—it is also about how strategically it uses the resources beneath it.

Some African countries show what is possible when this disconnect is addressed.

- Morocco, through OCP, has built a globally competitive phosphate-to-fertilizer industry while increasingly tailoring fertilizers to African soil conditions.
- Nigeria is leveraging its natural gas resources to expand domestic fertilizer production, significantly reducing imports and improving availability for farmers.

To scale these successes, a shift in priorities is required. Core policy actions include:

- Build local fertilizer and agro-input manufacturing, anchored in Africa’s own mineral resources
- Link mining, industrial, and agricultural policies, rather than treating them as separate silos
- Support regionally integrated value chains to achieve scale, reduce costs, and stabilize supply
- Use public procurement, financing, and regulation strategically to crowd in private investment

Unlocking Africa’s agricultural potential therefore requires a shift in policy focus—from acreage to capabilities and linkages.

Africa does not lack potential. It lacks coherent, integrated policy action to convert mineral wealth into productive agricultural systems and ultimately, into structural transformation.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah African Development Bank Group African Center for Economic Transformation (ACET)
